name: Mushroom World
family: Physical and model-driven: instruments, places, effects and composers built on simulators of fungal growth
lineage: The mushroom-substrate project (CrumpLabSandbox/mushroom-substrate): four simulators of mycelial growth and the web plugins built on them. No hardware or commercial lineage.
description: One fungus, many ways to hear it. Choose a species (90 real, 25 invented) and the size of simulator it was grown in. Two voices, each one of eight instruments built from the fungus (its network as a web of taut strings, its cap as a plate, its electrical model as an oscillator), played from the keys or by one of six composers that take their notes from a process of the fungus. An atmosphere plays underneath, an effect built from the same network takes the voices, and a small console brings it to a set loudness. Three world controls (growth, wetness, warmth) move every part at once.

hyphal-harp.name: Hyphal Harp
hyphal-harp.blurb: Pluck the network. Each note strikes the web of hyphae at a distance from its centre. The web is resized so its lowest mode is the key you play, and its own pattern of modes, worked out from its shape and the thickness of its cords, gives the tone. A hard strike wakes the high modes more than a soft one. While a key is held the web can go on growing, so the tone drifts toward that of the older network, and the old centre can be left to die back.

scales.4k: Only tips on a small bitmap: a young, thin web with no cords, so its modes come from shape alone. Nothing is abandoned, so dying back does nothing.
scales.40k: A flat colony with cords: thick cords pull the modes away from a plain string's.
scales.400k: A block of soil in three dimensions: the web the harp was first built on.
scales.4m: A plot metres across grown over years. Its real lowest note is below hearing, so it is shrunk much further to reach the key; the mode ratios are still its own.

cap-drums.name: Cap Drums
cap-drums.blurb: Each key is a mushroom cap of a different size, struck by a raindrop. A cap is treated as a small plate: the bigger it is, the lower it sounds. The species' fruit form sets the overtones, so a flat cap, a shelf, a cup and a ball each ring differently. How hard you hit a key is the size of the drop: a big drop is louder but lands more slowly, so it is a little duller. Each drop leaves water behind, so a cap played often gets wetter, lower and deader, and dries when left alone. A young cap can be played as a closed button that opens out.

scales.4k: No mushrooms grow at this size. The caps are worked out from the species' recorded size and form, and are always fully open.
scales.40k: Simple mushrooms grow, but there is no weather: the rain is whatever you play.
scales.400k: Mushrooms and weather: caps of the species' form, wetted by the drops you play.
scales.4m: Real-size mushrooms on a plot. The species' own cap size is reported so the drawing can mark its key.

spike-table.name: Spike Table
spike-table.blurb: A wavetable instrument. The table is one cycle of the voltage between two electrodes at each of 64 stages of the network's growth. A held note scans through the table, so the tone changes the way the electrical wave changed as the fungus grew. Each held note also moves on through growth by itself, a hard key starts later in growth than a soft one, the right ear can read a little later than the left, and the cycles can be made uneven in length.

scales.4k: No electrical model in the network. The table is one excitable unit alone, driven harder as the number of growing tips rises, so growth still changes the wave.
scales.40k: As at 4K: one unit alone, its drive following the tip count of the flat colony.
scales.400k: The full thing: voltage between two electrodes on a network whose electrical activity is modelled as it grows.
scales.4m: The same reading on a plot grown over years, so the table covers a much longer stretch of the network's life.

coupled-spikes.name: Coupled Spikes
coupled-spikes.blurb: The electrical model itself as the oscillator. Each note is a small ring of excitable units, the model the engines use for spiking, run fast enough to be heard and tuned so one cycle is the note. The units pull on their neighbours as stretches of hypha do. How hard they are driven, how unequal that is and how strongly they are coupled are the model's own settings, and here they are the timbre, along with how fast the units recover. A hard key drives the units harder, which changes the shape of the wave as well as its loudness. Temperature is set against the species' own coldest, best and hottest points: away from its best the drive weakens, and far enough away the units stop firing and the note falls silent.

scales.4k: The 4K engine has no electrical model or weather. The instrument runs its own ring of units, so it sounds the same; temperature is held at the species' best.
scales.40k: As at 4K: the ring is run here, and there is no weather to set a temperature.
scales.400k: The engine that has this electrical model and weather: temperature works, against the species' cardinal points.
scales.4m: The same as 400K. The plot's years of weather are not read; the temperature is the one you set.

turgor-bow.name: Turgor Bow
turgor-bow.blurb: The web sustained, not plucked. Hyphal tips do not grow smoothly: they advance in pulses. Here that pulsing is the bow. While a key is held, small strikes arrive at the pulse rate, a little irregular, with a faint hiss of smaller yields between them, and the web rings on under them. Several tips can pulse at once, each on its own clock, which turns the buzz into a texture. Temperature, set against the species' own coldest, best and hottest points, sets how fast they pulse. A hard key gives sudden, sharp pushes and a soft key slow, dull ones. The web can go on growing while the key is held.

scales.4k: Tips on a small bitmap, which is all this engine has: a young thin web with no cords, bowed by its tips. No weather, so temperature is held at the species' best.
scales.40k: A flat colony with cords, so the web's modes sit further from a plain string's. No weather, so temperature is held at the species' best.
scales.400k: A block of soil with weather: temperature works, against the species' cardinal points.
scales.4m: A plot metres across. Its real notes are below hearing, so the web is shrunk much further to reach the key; temperature works.

rhizomorph-bass.name: Rhizomorph Bass
rhizomorph-bass.blurb: One long cord as a string. A rhizomorph is not even along its length: it has thick and thin stretches. A wave travelling along it partly turns back wherever the thickness changes, so the cord rings with echoes inside it. Three stretches, two joints; how much turns back at each joint comes from the two cross-sections. A hard key is a sharp, narrow pluck and a soft key a broad, dull one. The middle of the cord can thicken while the note sounds, so the echoes grow in. An old cord has a hard rind, and a stiff cord sends its overtones sharp.

scales.4k: No cords at this size. The string is one even hypha: nothing turns back inside it, and the thickness controls do nothing. Rind and pluck still work.
scales.40k: Cords form where flow passes: the middle stretch is as thick as the species' thickest cord in a flat colony, and it can thicken as the note sounds.
scales.400k: Cords in a block of soil, as thick as the species' thickest there. Species that make no cords play as an even string.
scales.4m: Cords across a plot grown over years: the thickest cords, so the most turns back at each joint.

fairy-ring.name: Fairy Ring
fairy-ring.blurb: A ring of mycelium as a ring that carries a wave round and round. The living part of a fairy ring is a band: an outer edge advancing into fresh ground and an inner edge where it dies back. Each edge is a loop a little different in length, so the two beat. Every year the ring grows by the species' advance, and its note falls. Real rings are often broken in one place; a break splits each note into two close ones that beat. The disturbance that sets the ring going can reach all of it or only an arc, and a hard key is a sharper disturbance than a soft one.

scales.4k: A colony this size is millimetres across, not a ring. The ring is worked out from the species' tip speed alone.
scales.40k: As at 4K: no ring grows in the engine, so the advance is the tip speed kept up all year.
scales.400k: As at 4K and 40K: the block of soil is centimetres across. The advance is still the tip speed kept up all year.
scales.4m: A plot grown over years: the yearly advance is the one the plot itself showed, with its seasons, so the ring ages at a truer rate.

gill-comb.name: Gill Comb
gill-comb.blurb: The gills as a row of thin blades. Under a cap hang dozens of gills, each a thin plate fixed along its top edge. No two are quite the same length, so struck together they sound as a comb of close notes. As the cap opens the gills spread and their notes move apart. The species decides what hangs there: gills, spines, or the tubes of a bolete or bracket, which are air columns with their own overtones. Shorter gills between the full ones sound higher. Whatever strikes them can cross the row in time, so the comb is strummed from one side to the other, and a hard key bends the blades in their second way more.

scales.4k: No mushrooms grow at this size: what hangs under the cap is taken from the species' recorded form and size.
scales.40k: Simple mushrooms grow. The gills, spines or tubes follow the species' form.
scales.400k: Mushrooms in a block of soil. The gills, spines or tubes follow the species' form.
scales.4m: Real-size mushrooms: the count of gills a cap of the species' size would carry is reported for the drawing, though at most 16 sound.

spike-canon.name: Spike Canon
spike-canon.blurb: Rhythm and counterpoint from electrical activity. A short chain of excitable units, the model the engines use for spiking, runs live. The unit at the growing tip fires on its own; the ones behind it fire only when the wave reaches them. Each firing is a note, so the voices follow one another down the hypha like a canon. The tip's drive can come and go, so that spikes arrive in trains with quiet between, and the rate can follow the species' own spike interval.

scales.4k: No electrical activity is modelled at this size: each unit runs alone, so there is no canon, only pulses drifting against each other.
scales.40k: As at 4K: flow and cords exist, but no electrical network, so the units are uncoupled.
scales.400k: The full canon: the wave passes from the tip down a chain of coupled units.
scales.4m: Two individuals: the chain is two hyphae that do not join, each with its own tip, so two shorter canons run against each other.

hyphal-walk.name: Hyphal Walk
hyphal-walk.blurb: Melody from the shape of the network. Walkers travel it the way material moves through it, hop by hop along the hyphae, preferring the thicker cord at each junction. Every stop is a note: further from the centre is higher, a longer stretch is a longer note, a thicker cord is louder. A dead end is a rest, then the walker begins again from the centre. Some walkers can travel the other way, from a tip in to the centre, and the network can grow through its stages as it is walked.

scales.4k: A small young network with no cords and no flow: short outward phrases, loudness from how many ways lead on at each junction.
scales.40k: Cords and flow: walkers keep to thick cords, thicker is louder, and some can travel inward.
scales.400k: The same walk on a network grown in a block of soil.
scales.4m: A plot-size network over years: long routes along cords, and some phrases begin where a spore has founded a new individual.

tip-chorus.name: Tip Chorus
tip-chorus.blurb: Texture from branching. The growth rule itself runs live: tips advance across a field, branching at the species' rate and angle and fusing when two meet. Left to right across the field is low to high. The music starts as a few lines, thickens as the tips multiply, and thins where they fuse, crowd or leave. Temperature slows or stops the tips by the species' own curve.

scales.4k: This is the 4K engine's own subject: tips, branching and fusion, at a steady temperature.
scales.40k: The same, and in a cord-forming species a long-lived line grows louder as it thickens.
scales.400k: Adds temperature: the tips slow or stop by the species' curve.
scales.4m: Adds spores: new individuals are founded across the field every few seconds, and tips of different individuals do not fuse.

growth-form.name: Growth Form
growth-form.blurb: Large-scale form from a whole growth run. The species' prebuilt run is played through as one piece. How many notes sound follows the number of growing tips, loudness follows flow, note length follows the network's reserve. The notes are the network's real modes at each stage, all moved by one fixed interval, so the register falls as the network grows. Fusions sound as two neighbouring modes together and abandoned hyphae as a long quiet lowest mode, as often as the run had them.

scales.4k: A day or two of growth with no flow: loudness follows the front, note length the total length of hypha; fusions sound, nothing is abandoned.
scales.40k: Flow sets loudness and reserve sets note length; abandoned stretches are heard as the colony prunes itself.
scales.400k: The same form from a run in a block of soil.
scales.4m: Years of growth in one piece, with a new individual founded a third and two-thirds of the way through, each playing the modes of its own age.

season-cycle.name: Season Cycle
season-cycle.blurb: Form and dynamics from the year. The mycelium is active according to the species' own temperature curve: a slow line of low notes. Rain comes at random as a burst of quick high notes. Through the warm months the fungus stores reserve, and when autumn cools the ground below the species' fruiting temperature it fruits: each mushroom a short falling figure, stepping down the network's own notes as the cap expands, slower for a species with a bigger cap. The open caps then shed spores for a while. Winter is silence.

scales.4k: No weather, mushrooms or reserve: a steady temperature, and one line of low notes whose pace follows the number of growing tips.
scales.40k: No weather, but flow and simple mushrooms: the low line, and a flush of mushrooms whenever enough reserve is stored.
scales.400k: The full year: temperature, rain, reserve, and fruiting when autumn cools. No spores at this size.
scales.4m: Year after year, with spores: each year's spores can found a new individual, up to four, each working from its own note.

spore-scatter.name: Spore Scatter
spore-scatter.blurb: The spread of pitches from the spread of spores. Each note is a spore landing. Most fall close to the mushroom and a few travel far, by the same rule the stand-scale engine uses; distance on the ground is distance in pitch from a centre note. Rarely a far spore founds a new individual, and the centre moves there. The parent goes on shedding for a while, so two centres are heard at once.

scales.4k: No spores at this size: each note is a new branch placed inside the growing front, which widens through the run and begins again.
scales.40k: As at 4K: the simple mushrooms there shed no spores.
scales.400k: As at 4K: no spores are modelled in the block of soil.
scales.4m: Spores: most land close, a few far, and a far one can found a new individual and move the centre.

rain-on-caps.name: Rain on Caps
rain-on-caps.blurb: A square metre of ground with mushrooms on it, in real rain, in real time. Drops arrive at the true rate for the rainfall. A drop on a cap strikes that cap, a small plate whose notes depend on its size and form; a drop on the ground is a short thud in the soil. The drops are a mix of sizes, as in real rain, and the rain can come in showers. A key lets one drop fall on one cap: the biggest cap is the lowest key, and a harder press is a bigger drop.

scales.4k: No mushrooms grow at this size, so the caps are the species' recorded sizes only.
scales.40k: The caps are the species' recorded sizes and form; the rain is real rain, not the simulator's.
scales.400k: The same: caps from the species, real rain in real time.
scales.4m: The same. A square metre is a small corner of the plot at this size.

spore-cloud.name: Spore Cloud
spore-cloud.blurb: The sound of spores leaving. A mature cap sheds tens of thousands of spores a second, each launched at about a metre per second and pushing back on the cap as it goes. So many small random pushes make a steady hiss of force, and the cap, a small plate, answers at its own notes. Discharge rises and falls with the air, and stops when the air is too dry for the launching drop to form. Not every species sheds this way: cups, morels and clubs fire in puffs, and puffballs and bird's nests wait for a raindrop to knock the spores out.

scales.4k: No mushrooms or spores at this size: the caps are the species' recorded sizes and the spore rate is the published figure.
scales.40k: Simple mushrooms but no spores in the simulator: the rate is the published figure.
scales.400k: The same: the simulator does not follow spores at this size.
scales.4m: The only size whose simulator sheds spores. The sound is still made from the rate you set.

spike-chord.name: Spike Chord
spike-chord.blurb: A chord whose intervals are measurements. Five species have a measured interval between electrical spikes. Sped up by one factor, each becomes a pitch, and together they make a chord whose notes stand in the ratios of the data. Each voice is one unit of the engines' electrical model running at its species' rate. Under a second, much smaller speed-up the same intervals become a rhythm: each voice swells whenever a slow copy of its unit fires. The measured sizes of the spikes can set how loud each voice is. A key sets the pitch of the fastest voice, and so the speed-up for all of them.

scales.4k: No electrical activity at this size. The chord needs only each species' recorded interval, so it is unchanged.
scales.40k: As 4K: recorded intervals only.
scales.400k: The size whose simulator has electrical activity; the chord still uses the recorded intervals, not the simulated network.
scales.4m: As 400K.

decay.name: Decay
decay.blurb: A fallen log over years, heard as a wooden bar that raindrops strike. As fungi rot it the wood loses stiffness and weight. White rot takes everything together, so the note sinks slowly. Brown rot takes the cellulose and leaves the lignin: stiffness goes long before weight does, the note drops sharply, and the wood cracks into cubes. The fungus enters at one end and crosses the log at the pace of its own tips, so a slow species leaves one end soft and the other sound, and the bar's overtones drift apart. The species' own fruit bodies come out on the log as it goes, and the rain strikes them too.

scales.4k: Only the species' numbers are used: the rot spreads by tip speed, at the species' best temperature, and no fruit bodies appear.
scales.40k: As 4K, with fruit bodies on the log, and cord-formers crossing the log faster.
scales.400k: Everything: temperature sets the pace of rot, fruit bodies appear, cord-formers cross faster.
scales.4m: The same as 400K. The log is a metre of wood at every size.

after-rain.name: After Rain
after-rain.blurb: Electrical activity after rain. A column of excitable units runs from the surface down. Dry, they are at rest. Rain wets the top: the wet units are driven past their threshold and start to fire, and the firing passes down the column to the drier units below. As the ground dries, the surface first, the activity fades. The units run fast enough to be heard. How fast they fire follows the species: its own interval between spikes, and how near the ground is to the temperature it grows best at. A key makes it rain: a harder press is a heavier fall, and the key sets the rate of firing.

scales.4k: No weather, no electrical activity and no depth at this size: the units are borrowed from the 400K model, only three deep, at the species' best temperature, and the rain is yours.
scales.40k: As 4K: a flat colony, three units, borrowed electrical model.
scales.400k: The size this belongs to: a block of soil with depth, weather and electrical activity. All eight units and the temperature control.
scales.4m: As 400K.

forest-floor.name: Forest Floor
forest-floor.blurb: A colony growing live, heard as it grows. The simulator runs beside the sound. Every branch, fusion and abandoned hypha strikes the web of hyphae where it happened; about once a second the web is retuned to the network as it now is, so its notes fall as it grows. Mushrooms that begin to form ring as small plates while they expand. Between the strikes there is a faint steady push from all the growing tips at the edge. Rain strikes the ground and the mushrooms and leaves the ground wet, which deadens the web for a few seconds. A key taps the web yourself: low keys near the centre, high keys at the edge. When the block of soil is full, a new colony starts.

scales.4k: Only growth, branching and fusion: strikes and the push of the tips. No mushrooms, no rain. The tiny web is far above hearing at its real size, so its notes are lowered by whole octaves.
scales.40k: A flat colony: strikes, tips, pieces abandoned, and simple mushrooms. No rain.
scales.400k: A block of soil with weather: everything above, with rain and wet ground.
scales.4m: A plot metres across over years. Its notes are far below hearing and are raised by whole octaves. Mushrooms are real size, spores leaving shake their caps, and a new individual founded by a spore is heard starting.

foraging.name: Foraging
foraging.blurb: A cord-former searching soil for wood, live. As Forest Floor, with one more force: material moving through thick cords pushes on them, a steady push that only the web's lowest modes answer. While the fungus explores with thin hyphae this is silent. When it finds buried wood and the route to it thickens into cords carrying flow, a low tone swells under the strikes.

scales.4k: No flow and no cords at this size, so the low tone follows the number of growing tips. No mushrooms, no rain; the web's notes are lowered by whole octaves.
scales.40k: The size foraging belongs to: flow, thickening cords and die-back in a flat colony. The low tone is flow through cords.
scales.400k: The same in a block of soil, with rain and wet ground.
scales.4m: A plot metres across: the web's notes are raised by whole octaves; cords carry flow over metres, spores leave and found new individuals.

mycelium-reverb.name: Mycelium Reverb
mycelium-reverb.blurb: The room is a fungus. The sound going in shakes the network and you hear the network ring. Its resonances are the modes of the web of hyphae at the stage of growth you choose; two microphones at the surface give left and right. You choose where on the web the sound enters, from the centre to the growing edge, and the network can be left to grow while you listen.

scales.4k: A network about a centimetre across whose real notes are near the top of hearing; it is made bigger by whole octaves, and the factor is stated.
scales.40k: The flat colony of that simulator at its real size, cords included in its modes.
scales.400k: The network from the block of soil at its real size.
scales.4m: A network metres across and years old whose real notes are below hearing; it is made smaller by whole octaves, and the factor is stated. Growth while you listen covers years.

cord-delay.name: Cord Delay
cord-delay.blurb: Echoes that travel the cords. The six stretches of the network that hold the most material become six delay lines, each as long as the time to travel its stretch. Where one cord meets another of different thickness, part of a wave turns back: that reflection decides how much each line feeds the others. Each echo sits left to right where its cord really lies, thick cords keep more of the high sound, and a species that moves material faster gives quicker echoes.

scales.4k: No cords at this size: the six longest stretches of single hyphae, all one thickness, so echoes differ by length and place only.
scales.40k: The cords of the flat colony, with their real thickness and place.
scales.400k: The cords of the network in the block of soil; species that form no cords give six equal hyphae.
scales.4m: Cords metres long: the wave is taken ten or more times faster so the echoes fit in three seconds, and the page says by how much.

excitable-gate.name: Excitable Gate
excitable-gate.blurb: A gate that behaves like an excitable cell. The loudness of the sound going in is the drive on one unit of the engines' electrical model. Below its threshold nothing passes. Above it the unit fires: a spike that runs its full course whatever the input does, and lets the sound through while it lasts. Then it must recover before it can fire again. The unit can be the first of eight along a hypha, so the spike travels and the opening passes from the left ear to the right. The species sets the pace.

scales.4k: No electrical activity in that simulator: one unit on its own, paced by the species. The spike cannot travel.
scales.40k: No electrical activity in that simulator: one unit on its own, paced by the species. The spike cannot travel.
scales.400k: The unit can be the first of eight coupled along a hypha, as that simulator couples them, and the spike travels from left to right.
scales.4m: As at 400K: a single unit or a travelling spike along eight.

spore-granulator.name: Spore Granulator
spore-granulator.blurb: Your sound, thrown like spores. The sound going in is kept for two seconds. Grains of it are launched at a rate set by the size of the species' cap. Each grain lasts a spore's flight time, and how far back in the kept sound it is taken from follows the rule for how far spores land: most from just now, a few from long ago. Wind pushes grains to one side. Cup fungi, morels, puffballs and bird's nests let go in puffs. Air drag can bend each grain's pitch as it slows.

scales.4k: No mushrooms grow in that simulator: the cap is the species' recorded size. Grains are launched from one place only.
scales.40k: The simple mushrooms of that simulator set the rate by their cap. Grains are launched from one place only.
scales.400k: As at 40K: the cap sets the rate, one launch place.
scales.4m: Spores are followed there and can found new individuals: a grain that lands far away starts a second launch place, further back in time and to one side, for about two seconds.

rot-filter.name: Rot Filter
rot-filter.blurb: Your sound through a rotting log. The sound going in drives a wooden bar. As the bar rots it loses stiffness and weight, so its notes fall and blur. White rot takes both together; brown rot takes stiffness first, and the notes drop sharply. Left alone the log rots while you listen, at a pace set by the species, the wetness of the wood and the temperature, and when it has gone another falls.

scales.4k: No weather in that simulator: the log rots at the species' best temperature, and the temperature control is off.
scales.40k: No weather in that simulator: the log rots at the species' best temperature, and the temperature control is off.
scales.400k: Temperature sets the pace of rot through the species' own temperature curve.
scales.4m: As at 400K. The years that simulator covers are the scale a real log rots on; here they are still squeezed into seconds.

soil-filter.name: Soil Filter
soil-filter.blurb: Sound heard through soil. Soil swallows sound, the high notes first, and more so the longer the way through it and the wetter the ground. The sound also arrives late, by the time it takes to travel. Two listeners sit 10 cm apart, so a source off to one side reaches them at different times and with different dullness. Rain wets the ground from the top down. The listener can be the species' own network, shaken by what comes through. This is what a truffle would hear.

scales.4k: That simulator is flat and has no weather: the distance is taken sideways through the top layer, it does not rain, and the listening network is made bigger by whole octaves to be heard.
scales.40k: That simulator is flat and has no weather: the distance is taken sideways through the top layer and it does not rain. The network listens at its real size.
scales.400k: A block of soil with depth and weather: the listener is under the surface, rain wets the ground from the top, and the network listens at its real size.
scales.4m: Depth and weather as at 400K. The network is metres across, so it is made smaller by whole octaves to be heard, and the page says by how much.

parameters.name: Species
parameters.description: The fungus everything is built from: its network, its fruit body, its numbers. The last 25 are invented, not real.

parameters.name: Scale
parameters.description: The size of simulator the specimen was grown in. Each is a different kind of model; some processes do not exist at some sizes.

parameters.name: Growth
parameters.description: How grown the network is, from first threads to its full recorded size. Moves the stage of growth in every part that has one.

parameters.name: Wet
parameters.description: How wet the ground, the air and the caps are. Moves wetness, humidity and soaking in every part that has them.

parameters.name: Warmth
parameters.description: Temperature, in degrees from the species' best. Moves temperature in every part that has it; outside the species' limits those parts stop.

parameters.name: Instrument
parameters.description: Which instrument this voice is.

parameters.name: Played by
parameters.description: Keys: you play it. Otherwise a composer plays it from a process of the fungus.

parameters.name: Octave
parameters.description: Moves this voice by whole octaves.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: This voice's fader into the master; -60 is silence.

parameters.name: Pan
parameters.description: Left to right.

parameters.name: Instrument
parameters.description: Which instrument this voice is.

parameters.name: Played by
parameters.description: Keys: you play it. Otherwise a composer plays it from a process of the fungus.

parameters.name: Octave
parameters.description: Moves this voice by whole octaves.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: This voice's fader into the master; -60 is silence.

parameters.name: Pan
parameters.description: Left to right.

parameters.name: Atmosphere
parameters.description: A place that plays by itself under the voices.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: The atmosphere's fader; -60 is silence.

parameters.name: Effect
parameters.description: What the voices are sent through.

parameters.name: Send
parameters.description: How much of the voices goes into the effect.

parameters.name: Return
parameters.description: How loud the effect comes back.

parameters.name: Target
parameters.description: The loudness the master is ridden to.

parameters.name: Ceiling
parameters.description: The limiter's ceiling.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Output level after the limiter.

parameters.name: Stage of growth
parameters.description: Which of eight snapshots of the growing network supplies the modes. A young web is small and simple; an old one has cords and loops.

parameters.name: Where it is struck
parameters.description: Distance from the centre, in six rings. Each mode is driven by how much the web moves there in that mode.

parameters.name: Its own modes
parameters.description: At 100% the overtones are the network's own, set by its shape and cord thickness. At 0% they are a plain string's.

parameters.name: Grows while held
parameters.description: While a key is held the network goes on growing from the chosen stage toward the end of its run, and its modes move with it. Real growth takes days.

parameters.name: Dying back at the centre
parameters.description: Old hyphae at the centre are abandoned as the colony moves out. Modes that move mostly in the two inner rings lose loudness and ring time by their share of movement there.
parameters.standing: from the model; the amount is a choice

parameters.name: Ring time
parameters.description: How long the web rings. Real hyphae are damped almost at once; the true value is near zero.

parameters.name: High modes ring as long
parameters.description: How much faster the higher modes die away than the lowest.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Loudness only.

parameters.name: Ring time
parameters.description: How long a struck cap rings. Real caps are damped almost at once.

parameters.name: How wet the cap is
parameters.description: A soaked cap carries water: it is heavier, so up to 6% lower, and more damped.

parameters.name: Water each drop leaves
parameters.description: Each drop adds to the wetness of the cap it hits, a big drop more. The water dries away over about six seconds, so a cap played often goes lower and deader and then recovers.

parameters.name: How far the cap has opened
parameters.description: A young cap is a closed button, close to a ball. As it expands it takes the species' own form, and its overtones move from a ball's to that form's.

parameters.name: Where the drop lands
parameters.description: A hit at the centre wakes different overtones from a hit at the rim.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Loudness only.

parameters.name: Stage of growth
parameters.description: Where in the table the note reads: the shape the voltage had at that stage of the network's growth.

parameters.name: Drift through growth
parameters.description: How fast the reading point drifts back and forth through the stages.

parameters.name: How far it drifts
parameters.description: How much of the table the drift covers.

parameters.name: Each note grows
parameters.description: While a key is held, that note reads further and further on in the network's growth, on top of the shared drift.

parameters.name: A hard key reads later
parameters.description: How far the force on the key moves the starting point: a hard key begins later in growth, a soft key earlier. A key at 0.8 is not moved.

parameters.name: Right ear reads later
parameters.description: The left ear hears the wave at the note's stage of growth, the right ear the wave from a little later, up to a quarter of the table.

parameters.name: Uneven spike intervals
parameters.description: Recorded intervals between spikes are far from even. Each cycle is made longer or shorter than the key's by a random share, which roughens the note and at the top turns it to noise.
parameters.standing: sourced, contested; the amount is a choice

parameters.name: Attack
parameters.description: How fast a note comes in.

parameters.name: Release
parameters.description: How fast it dies away.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Loudness only.

parameters.name: Units in the ring
parameters.description: How many stretches of hypha are modelled, joined in a ring and spread left to right.

parameters.name: Drive
parameters.description: How hard the units are pushed. In the engines, growing tips are driven hardest. It changes the wave's shape between slow build and sharp spike.

parameters.name: Unequal drive
parameters.description: How different the units' drives are. Unequal units beat against each other.

parameters.name: Coupling
parameters.description: How strongly each unit pulls on its neighbours. Strong coupling locks them together; weak coupling lets them drift.

parameters.name: Recovery
parameters.description: How fast a unit recovers after firing. The engines use 0.08. Slow recovery gives a long rest and a brief spike, which is a thin, bright wave; fast recovery gives a rounder one.

parameters.name: A hard key drives harder
parameters.description: How much the force on the key adds to the drive. A key at 0.8 gives the drive as set.

parameters.name: Temperature
parameters.description: Activity follows the species' temperature curve: full at its best temperature, none at its coldest and hottest. Here it scales the drive, so away from its best the wave softens and then stops.
parameters.standing: curve from the species; its effect on spiking assumed

parameters.name: Attack
parameters.description: How fast a note comes in.

parameters.name: Release
parameters.description: How fast it dies away.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Loudness only.

parameters.name: Growth pulses
parameters.description: How often the tips pulse. Measured at 2.7 to 14 a minute; sped up here.

parameters.name: How irregular the pulses are
parameters.description: Real pulses are not evenly spaced.

parameters.name: Tips pulsing
parameters.description: How many growing tips push on the web, each pulsing on its own clock. A real colony has hundreds to thousands; the count at this stage is shown in the drawing's data.

parameters.name: Temperature
parameters.description: Growth follows the species' temperature curve: fastest at its best temperature, stopped at its coldest and hottest. The pulse rate is scaled by that curve, so far from its best the bow slows and then stops.
parameters.standing: curve from the species; its effect on pulsing assumed

parameters.name: Turgor
parameters.description: The pressure inside the hyphae. More pressure, a harder push at each pulse.

parameters.name: Stage of growth
parameters.description: Which snapshot of the network supplies the modes.

parameters.name: Grows while held
parameters.description: While a key is held the network goes on growing from the chosen stage, and its modes move with it.

parameters.name: Where the tips are
parameters.description: Distance from the centre at which the pulsing acts. Tips are at the edge of a growing colony.

parameters.name: Its own modes
parameters.description: At 100% the overtones are the network's own; at 0% a plain string's.

parameters.name: Ring time
parameters.description: How long the web rings between pulses.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Loudness only.

parameters.name: Thick against thin
parameters.description: How much thicker the middle stretch is than the ends, up to the species' thickest cord. More contrast, more of the wave turns back at each joint.

parameters.name: Where the cord thickens
parameters.description: Where along the cord the thick stretch begins and ends. This places the echoes.

parameters.name: Where it is plucked
parameters.description: Where the cord is disturbed.

parameters.name: Thickens as it sounds
parameters.description: A cord thickens where flow keeps passing. The note starts on an even cord and the middle stretch reaches its full thickness after this long, so the echoes grow in. A cord with a thick middle sounds higher than an even one of the same length, so the note starts up to a fourth low and rises to the key as it thickens.

parameters.name: Stiff rind
parameters.description: An old rhizomorph has a hard dark rind. A stiff cord carries high notes faster than low ones, so its overtones go sharp of a plain string's. High keys take less, because a short cord cannot hold as much.

parameters.name: Ring time
parameters.description: How long it rings. Real cords are damped almost at once.

parameters.name: High notes kept
parameters.description: How much of the high end survives each trip along the cord.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Loudness only.

parameters.name: Age of the ring
parameters.description: Each year the radius grows by the species' advance, the loop lengthens and the note falls.

parameters.name: Width of the living band
parameters.description: The outer edge is longer than the inner by this much radius, so the two loops are slightly out of tune and beat. Measured mats are 4 to 22 cm deep; bands vary.

parameters.name: A break in the ring
parameters.description: Rings are often broken where they met a path, a root or another ring. Waves that move at the break are held back there, and waves that are still at it pass freely, so every note splits into two close ones that beat. A bigger break, a wider split.
parameters.standing: physics, simplified; the amount is a choice

parameters.name: How much of the ring is disturbed
parameters.description: The note starts with random pushes on the ring, like a shower. All round, it starts as a wash; on a short arc, the same burst comes past again each lap, which is buzzier and brighter.

parameters.name: Ring time
parameters.description: How long the wave keeps going round.

parameters.name: High notes kept
parameters.description: How much of the high end survives each lap.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Loudness only.

parameters.name: Gills
parameters.description: How many gills sound. A real cap has tens to hundreds.

parameters.name: How far the cap has opened
parameters.description: As the cap opens the gills fan out and differ more in length, so their notes spread.

parameters.name: The blade's second bend
parameters.description: A blade fixed at one edge has a second way of bending, 6.27 times higher, and a third at 17.55. For tubes these are the air column's overtones, 3 and 5 times. A hard key wakes them more.

parameters.name: Short gills between
parameters.description: Between the full gills hang shorter ones that do not reach the stem. Every second gill is made shallower, down to seven tenths; a blade's note rises as one over its depth squared, so at the limit it is an octave higher.

parameters.name: Time to cross the gills
parameters.description: Whatever strikes the gills, a drop running across or a draught, reaches them one after another from one side. At zero they are all struck together.

parameters.name: Ring time
parameters.description: How long the gills ring.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Loudness only.

parameters.name: Units along the hypha
parameters.description: How many stretches of hypha are modelled, tip first. Each is a voice.

parameters.name: Spike rate at the tip
parameters.description: How often the driven tip unit fires. In life this is the species' spike interval; here it is sped up.

parameters.name: Coupling along the hypha
parameters.description: How strongly each unit pulls on its neighbours. Too weak and the wave dies before it reaches the far end.

parameters.name: How much harder the tip is driven
parameters.description: Growing tips are the pacemakers. At 0% no unit fires by itself; at 100% several do, and the canon breaks into cross-rhythm.

parameters.name: Recovery
parameters.description: How fast a unit can fire again. Slower recovery makes units skip beats.

parameters.name: Stage of growth for the notes
parameters.description: Which snapshot of the network supplies the notes: unit k plays the network's k-th mode.

parameters.name: Lowest note
parameters.description: Where the network's lowest mode is put. Everything else follows from its ratios.

parameters.name: Note length
parameters.description: How long each note is held.

parameters.name: Spike trains
parameters.description: In the recordings spikes come in trains with quiet stretches between. This makes the tip's drive rise and fall once in about sixteen spikes; at 100% the chain is silent for over half of each turn.

parameters.name: Follow the species' spike interval
parameters.description: At 100% the rate is multiplied by 60 minutes over the species' recorded interval, so a species that spikes twice as often plays twice as fast. Held between 0.1 and 12 a second.

parameters.name: Modes closer than this are one note
parameters.description: A dense network has many modes at almost the same frequency. Those nearer than this to the one below are counted once, so the voices are not all on one pitch. At 0 every mode is used.

parameters.name: Register
parameters.description: Moves every note by whole octaves. The intervals between the network's notes are kept.

parameters.name: Share of notes heard
parameters.description: The process runs the same; only this share of its events is sounded, picked at random. For playing alongside other composers.

parameters.name: Travel speed
parameters.description: How fast a walker covers a stretch of average length. In life transport runs at millimetres to centimetres an hour.

parameters.name: Preference for thick cords
parameters.description: At a junction the odds of each way out go as cord thickness to this power. At 0 every way is equally likely; high values keep to the trunk routes.

parameters.name: Walkers
parameters.description: How many travel at once. Each is a voice.

parameters.name: Rest at a dead end
parameters.description: A tip is a dead end. The phrase ends there and a new one starts from the centre.

parameters.name: Stage of growth
parameters.description: Which snapshot of the network is walked. A young one gives short phrases; an old one, long routes along cords.

parameters.name: Lowest note
parameters.description: Where the centre of the network is put.

parameters.name: How much of each stretch sounds
parameters.description: Note length as a share of the time taken to travel the stretch.

parameters.name: Walkers travelling inward
parameters.description: What the tips take up is carried back toward the centre, so transport runs both ways. This share of the walkers start at a tip in the outer half and only take ways that lead nearer the centre, sounding each place as they leave it: falling phrases that end when no way leads further in.

parameters.name: Grow through the stages in
parameters.description: The network's eight stored stages of growth are walked in turn over this time, starting from the stage above, then again from the youngest. Routes and notes change at each stage.

parameters.name: Modes closer than this are one note
parameters.description: A dense network has many modes at almost the same frequency. Those nearer than this to the one below are counted once, so the voices are not all on one pitch. At 0 every mode is used.

parameters.name: Register
parameters.description: Moves every note by whole octaves. The intervals between the network's notes are kept.

parameters.name: Share of notes heard
parameters.description: The process runs the same; only this share of its events is sounded, picked at random. For playing alongside other composers.

parameters.name: Tip speed
parameters.description: How fast tips advance. One step is 0.1 mm; in life a tip takes minutes to hours over it.

parameters.name: Branching
parameters.description: Multiplies the species' branching rate (one branch per growth unit of hypha, per tip).

parameters.name: Branch angle
parameters.description: Multiplies the species' branch angle. Wide angles spread the voices across the pitch range; narrow ones keep them in a bundle.

parameters.name: Fusion
parameters.description: Multiplies the chance that two tips that meet become one. A fusion sounds an octave lower.

parameters.name: Room for tips
parameters.description: Crowding: branching slows as the field fills, and stops at this many tips.

parameters.name: A tip sounds every
parameters.description: How often an advancing tip is heard between branches.

parameters.name: Centre note
parameters.description: The pitch of the middle of the field, where growth starts.

parameters.name: Width of the field
parameters.description: How much pitch the 12.8 mm field covers.

parameters.name: Note length
parameters.description: How long each note is held.

parameters.name: Temperature, from the species' best
parameters.description: Tip speed follows the species' temperature curve between its lowest, best and highest temperatures. Away from the best the tips slow; outside the limits they stop and the music stops with them.

parameters.name: Pull toward the network's own notes
parameters.description: Moves each note's distance from the centre note toward the nearest interval that the network's modes make with its lowest mode.

parameters.name: Register
parameters.description: Moves every note by whole octaves. The intervals between the network's notes are kept.

parameters.name: Share of notes heard
parameters.description: The process runs the same; only this share of its events is sounded, picked at random. For playing alongside other composers.

parameters.name: Length of the piece
parameters.description: The whole growth run is played in this time, then begins again.

parameters.name: Notes per growing tip
parameters.description: Scales how many notes the tip count produces.

parameters.name: Where the grown network's lowest mode is put
parameters.description: One fixed interval moves every real mode frequency into reach. Their relations to each other are kept.

parameters.name: Highest note allowed
parameters.description: The young network's modes are very high; anything above this is brought down by whole octaves until it fits.

parameters.name: Fusions and abandonments heard
parameters.description: For each stage the run counted branches, fusions and abandoned stretches per hour. A fusion sounds two neighbouring modes together; an abandonment sounds the lowest mode, quiet and long. Each takes the place of an ordinary note as often as it happened against branching.

parameters.name: Register
parameters.description: Moves every note by whole octaves. The intervals between the network's notes are kept.

parameters.name: Share of notes heard
parameters.description: The process runs the same; only this share of its events is sounded, picked at random. For playing alongside other composers.

parameters.name: Length of a year
parameters.description: One year of seasons in this time.

parameters.name: Climate
parameters.description: Shifts the yearly mean, which starts 8 °C below the species' optimum. Too cold and it never grows; too warm and it never fruits.

parameters.name: Summer to winter
parameters.description: How far the temperature swings through the year.

parameters.name: Rain
parameters.description: How often it rains. Rain wakes activity for a while, as the electrical recordings after rain suggest.

parameters.name: Lowest note
parameters.description: Where the network's lowest mode is put.

parameters.name: Spores heard after fruiting
parameters.description: Open caps shed spores for days. After each flush a thinning shower of very short, quiet, high notes is heard, more of them for more caps and in damp air. A tiny sample of the real number.

parameters.name: Modes closer than this are one note
parameters.description: A dense network has many modes at almost the same frequency. Those nearer than this to the one below are counted once, so the voices are not all on one pitch. At 0 every mode is used.

parameters.name: Register
parameters.description: Moves every note by whole octaves. The intervals between the network's notes are kept.

parameters.name: Share of notes heard
parameters.description: The process runs the same; only this share of its events is sounded, picked at random. For playing alongside other composers.

parameters.name: Spores heard
parameters.description: A tiny sample of the real discharge, which is about 30,000 a second from one cap.

parameters.name: Middling landing distance
parameters.description: Half the spores land nearer than this. On the ground the engine uses 8 cm.

parameters.name: Wind
parameters.description: Pushes more spores to one side.

parameters.name: How much discharge comes and goes
parameters.description: Spore release depends on humidity and moving air, so it arrives in waves.

parameters.name: Founding
parameters.description: How readily a spore that lands far out founds a new individual, which moves the centre. In the engine this is rare.

parameters.name: Centre note
parameters.description: Where the first mushroom stands.

parameters.name: Note length
parameters.description: How long each landing sounds.

parameters.name: Parent keeps shedding for about
parameters.description: After a spore founds a new individual, the old mushroom does not stop at once. Its share of the spores heard falls away over this time, so the old and new centres overlap.

parameters.name: Pull toward the network's own notes
parameters.description: Moves each landing distance toward the nearest interval that the network's modes make with its lowest mode. Spores that land beyond the largest are left where they fell.

parameters.name: Register
parameters.description: Moves every note by whole octaves. The intervals between the network's notes are kept.

parameters.name: Share of notes heard
parameters.description: The process runs the same; only this share of its events is sounded, picked at random. For playing alongside other composers.

parameters.name: Rainfall
parameters.description: Sets how many drops fall per square metre per second: rainfall divided by the volume of one drop. Light rain is 2, heavy is 20 and more.

parameters.name: Drop size
parameters.description: A bigger drop is heavier and falls faster, so it hits harder, and for the same rainfall there are fewer of them.

parameters.name: Mix of drop sizes
parameters.description: Real rain has many small drops and a few large ones, falling off exponentially with size (Marshall and Palmer, 1948). At 0 every drop is the same size. The number of drops is corrected so the rainfall stays what you set.

parameters.name: Showers
parameters.description: Rain comes in cells that pass over in a minute or so. This is how far the rain thins between them; the caps dry a little and ring longer and higher in the gaps.

parameters.name: Mushrooms
parameters.description: How many fruiting bodies stand in the square metre. Sizes are drawn from the species' range.

parameters.name: Cap size
parameters.description: Scales every cap. Smaller caps are higher and, being lighter, louder for the same drop.

parameters.name: Ring time
parameters.description: How long a struck cap rings. Wet caps ring shorter and lower as they take on water.

parameters.name: Ground
parameters.description: How loud drops on bare ground are beside drops on caps.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Loudness only.

parameters.name: Spores leaving each cap
parameters.description: About 30,000 a second is reported; up to 140,000 for some species. More launches make a stronger, smoother hiss.

parameters.name: Launch speed
parameters.description: Measured launch speeds run from 0.1 to 1.8 m/s. A faster launch pushes back harder.

parameters.name: How much discharge comes and goes
parameters.description: Discharge depends on humidity and moving air, so each cap's output swells and fades.

parameters.name: How the spores leave
parameters.description: Gilled and pored fruit bodies launch each spore from a drop of water. Cups, morels and clubs fire many spore sacs together in a puff. A puffball or bird's nest sheds when a raindrop lands on it: over a million spores in a hundredth of a second is reported for one drop on a puffball.

parameters.name: Humidity of the air
parameters.description: A launched spore is thrown by a drop of water that condenses on it. In dry air the drop does not form and discharge stops. Rain-knocked spores do not care.

parameters.name: Length of a day
parameters.description: The air is damp at night and up to 25 points drier at midday, so discharge follows the day. Lower the humidity a little to hear midday fall quiet.
parameters.standing: sped up; the daily swing is assumed

parameters.name: Mushrooms
parameters.description: How many caps are shedding, spread left to right.

parameters.name: Cap size
parameters.description: Scales every cap. Smaller caps answer higher.

parameters.name: Ring time
parameters.description: How sharply each cap picks out its notes from the hiss.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Loudness only.

parameters.name: Pitch of the fastest
parameters.description: Sets the one speed-up applied to every species. The fastest is the split gill, one spike every 41 minutes.

parameters.name: Schizophyllum commune
parameters.description: Measured interval between spikes: 41 minutes (extracellular recordings).

parameters.name: Pleurotus ostreatus
parameters.description: Measured interval between spikes: 70 minutes (extracellular recordings).

parameters.name: Omphalotus nidiformis
parameters.description: Measured interval between spikes: 92 minutes (extracellular recordings).

parameters.name: Flammulina velutipes
parameters.description: Measured interval between spikes: 102 minutes (extracellular recordings).

parameters.name: Cordyceps militaris
parameters.description: Measured interval between spikes: 116 minutes (extracellular recordings).

parameters.name: The loaded species
parameters.description: The species chosen above, at its own spike interval.

parameters.name: Loudness from the measured spike size
parameters.description: The recorded spikes differ in size: 0.03 mV for the split gill, 0.5 for the oyster, 0.007 for the ghost fungus, 0.3 for enoki, 0.2 for Cordyceps. At 100% each voice is as loud as its spike is large beside the largest.

parameters.name: Rhythm of the fastest
parameters.description: A second speed-up of the same intervals. A slow copy of each unit fires at this rate for the fastest species and in the measured ratios for the rest; a voice is up while its copy is firing.

parameters.name: Drive
parameters.description: How hard each unit is pushed: the shape of the wave.

parameters.name: How much the intervals wander
parameters.description: Real spike intervals vary from one spike to the next.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Loudness only.

parameters.name: How far gone
parameters.description: How far the rot has got: the end where the fungus came in is furthest gone, the far end least. Sets stiffness and weight along the log, and so each note of the bar.

parameters.name: Time for the log to go
parameters.description: A wood-rotter at its best temperature takes this long, then a fresh log falls. Colder or hotter, or a species that is not a wood-rotter, takes longer. In the field this takes decades.

parameters.name: Kind of rot
parameters.description: White rot removes lignin and cellulose together. Brown rot removes cellulose and leaves lignin, so the wood loses its strength early and cracks.

parameters.name: Temperature
parameters.description: The rot goes at the pace the species grows at this temperature: nothing below its coldest or above its hottest, fastest at its best. Each species has its own three temperatures.
parameters.standing: from the species; the curve is a research estimate

parameters.name: Fruit bodies on the log
parameters.description: Once the fungus is established its fruit bodies come out one after another and expand, at the species' recorded size and form. Rain strikes them by their share of the area.
parameters.standing: a choice; sizes from the species

parameters.name: Length of the log
parameters.description: A longer bar is lower, as one over its length squared.

parameters.name: Drops landing on it
parameters.description: What strikes the log.

parameters.name: Ring time when sound
parameters.description: How long sound wood rings. Rot shortens it.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Loudness only.

parameters.name: Rain
parameters.description: How often it rains.

parameters.name: Time to dry
parameters.description: How long the ground stays wet, and so how long the activity lasts. In life, hours to days.

parameters.name: How far the water soaks
parameters.description: How much of the wetness reaches each deeper unit.

parameters.name: Coupling down the column
parameters.description: How strongly firing above stirs the units below.

parameters.name: Rate of firing
parameters.description: How fast a driven unit fires, for a species that spikes once an hour, at its best temperature. In the recordings, minutes to hours; sped up here.

parameters.name: Temperature of the ground
parameters.description: Firing is fastest at the temperature the species grows best at and slows toward its coldest and hottest. Each species has its own three temperatures.
parameters.standing: from the species; the link to firing is assumed

parameters.name: Spikes between rains
parameters.description: In the recordings a fungus left alone still spikes now and then. Here one unit fires once on its own and the spike passes along the column; a species with a shorter interval does it more often.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Loudness only.

parameters.name: Growth speed
parameters.description: How fast the simulator runs. One step is the time a tip takes to grow 0.1 mm: minutes to hours of real time.

parameters.name: Ring time
parameters.description: How long the web rings after a strike.

parameters.name: Size of everything that rings
parameters.description: Scales every note. At real size a young network is very high.

parameters.name: Push of the growing tips
parameters.description: Each tip grows in small pulses, each a push at the edge of the web. Many tips at random add up to a steady push whose strength goes as the square root of their number, taken live from the simulator. Each mode answers by how much it moves at the edge.
parameters.standing: from the model, with an assumed link

parameters.name: Stage of growth
parameters.description: Which snapshots of the growing network supply the resonances. The two nearest are cross-faded.

parameters.name: Size of the network
parameters.description: Scales every resonance. A network twice as big rings an octave lower.

parameters.name: Ring time
parameters.description: How long the web rings after the sound stops. Real hyphae are damped almost at once.

parameters.name: High modes die sooner
parameters.description: Extra damping of the higher resonances.

parameters.name: Where the sound enters
parameters.description: The web is divided into six rings from the centre to the edge. Each mode is driven by how much it moves in the ring where the sound enters, so the old centre and the young edge wake different resonances.

parameters.name: Growth while you listen
parameters.description: Moves through the stored stages of the run on its own, from a young network to the full-grown one, so the resonances fall as the web spreads. Starts from the stage set above.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Loudness only.

parameters.name: Stage of growth
parameters.description: Which snapshot of the network supplies the cords. Older networks have longer, thicker ones.

parameters.name: Travel time
parameters.description: How long a wave takes to cover a millimetre of cord. This sets every echo from the cords' real lengths.

parameters.name: How much turns back
parameters.description: Scales the reflection at each junction, which itself comes from the change in thickness there.

parameters.name: Loss along the cord
parameters.description: High frequencies are lost each time round, as a wave in a soft tube would lose them. A thick cord loses less than a thin one.

parameters.name: How much the cords have thickened
parameters.description: Cords thicken where material flows through them. This raises or lowers every cross-section as a power, from all alike to twice as contrasted as grown, which changes which cords are chosen, how much turns back between them and how bright each echo stays.
parameters.standing: from the model, exaggerated by choice

parameters.name: Species' own speed
parameters.description: Species move material along their cords at 10 to 20 mm an hour. The wave is taken faster in the same proportion, measured against 14 mm an hour, so a fast species gives quicker echoes.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Loudness only.

parameters.name: Threshold
parameters.description: How loud the sound must be before the unit fires over and over. A sudden sound a third as loud can still set off one spike.

parameters.name: Speed of the unit
parameters.description: How fast the unit lives: a spike and its recovery take one cycle. In life, minutes to hours.

parameters.name: Species sets the pace
parameters.description: The speed is multiplied by 70 minutes over the species' measured interval between spikes, so a slow-spiking species gives a slower gate.

parameters.name: How much of the spike lets sound through
parameters.description: The gate is open while the unit's voltage is above a level; this moves the level from the very tip of the spike to the whole of it.

parameters.name: Gate follows the spike's shape
parameters.description: At 0 the gate is open or shut. At 100% the loudness follows the unit's voltage itself: a fast rise, a slow sag, a sudden fall.

parameters.name: How far the spike travels
parameters.description: Eight units coupled in a row as the engines couple them along a hypha. The left ear hears the gate at the first unit, the right ear the gate further along, so the opening crosses from left to right at the speed the spike travels.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Loudness only.

parameters.name: Grains launched
parameters.description: A real cap launches about 30,000 spores a second; this is a thousandth of that, for a cap of 5 cm radius.

parameters.name: Cap of the species sets the rate
parameters.description: Spores come from the gill surface, which goes with the square of the cap's radius. A bigger cap launches more grains a second.

parameters.name: Launch speed
parameters.description: Measured launch speeds are 0.1 to 1.8 m/s. A faster launch flies longer, so the grain is longer.

parameters.name: Slowed by the air
parameters.description: A spore leaves fast and the air stops it almost at once. Each grain is read faster at first and settles to true speed, so its pitch starts high and falls.

parameters.name: Middling landing distance
parameters.description: Half the grains come from more recently than this. On the ground the engine uses 8 cm.

parameters.name: Puffs
parameters.description: Gilled mushrooms launch spores one by one, steadily. Cup fungi fire thousands of spore sacs at once and puffballs puff when a raindrop hits. The same number of grains, gathered into bursts.

parameters.name: Far spores found new individuals
parameters.description: A spore that lands more than three times the middling distance away can start a new individual, which then launches grains from its own place and time for about two seconds.
parameters.standing: from the model, largest simulator only

parameters.name: Wind
parameters.description: Pushes the grains to one side.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Loudness only.

parameters.name: How far gone
parameters.description: The share of the log that has rotted. Sets stiffness and weight, and so every resonance. If the log is rotting as you listen, this is where it starts from.

parameters.name: Rotting while you listen
parameters.description: What is left of the log goes at a steady share per second, the usual way decay is described. The time is for a wood-rotting species at its best temperature in half-wet wood; other species and conditions are slower.

parameters.name: Wetness of the wood
parameters.description: Water makes the log heavier, so its notes are lower, and it rings for less time. Rot needs water but also air: it stops in dry wood and in waterlogged wood, and is fastest about half way.

parameters.name: Temperature
parameters.description: The pace of rot follows the species' temperature curve: nothing below its coldest or above its hottest, fastest at its best.

parameters.name: Kind of rot
parameters.description: White rot removes lignin and cellulose together. Brown rot leaves the lignin and the wood loses its strength early.

parameters.name: Length of the log
parameters.description: A longer bar is lower, as one over its length squared.

parameters.name: Ring time when sound
parameters.description: How long sound wood rings. Rot and water shorten it.

parameters.name: Level
parameters.description: Loudness only.

parameters.name: Depth of the listener
parameters.description: How much soil the sound passes through. Litter and organic soil hold most mycelium; truffles fruit at 5 to 30 cm.

parameters.name: Wetness of the soil
parameters.description: Wet soil damps high sound more strongly.

parameters.name: Rain
parameters.description: While it rains a wet front moves down from the surface and the soil above it is wetter, so a deep listener hears the dulling arrive late. When the rain stops the water drains and the sound clears.

parameters.name: Source off to one side
parameters.description: Two listeners 10 cm apart, as two parts of one mycelium. A source to one side has a shorter way to the nearer one: it arrives there sooner, louder and brighter.

parameters.name: Heard by the network
parameters.description: What comes through the soil shakes the species' full-grown network, and its two microphones hear the network's own modes ring. Wet soil damps them.
parameters.standing: from the model, ring time a choice
